messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi Mensah is a 22-year-old man of Ghanaian descent who works as a school principal, a role that places him, daily, in a position of authority over children whose safety and stability depend on the adults around them. The particular weight of that responsibility is not lost on him. He came to his first intake session dressed carefully, speaking in measured sentences, and it was only gradually — across several meetings — that the shape of what he carries began to emerge.

Kofi grew up in a household governed by a caregiver whose moods shifted without warning. The physical abuse was not ritualistic or predictable; it arrived in the spaces between ordinary moments — a meal, a homework assignment, a noise in the hallway — and that randomness was itself a kind of violence. He learned early that the environment could turn without signal. A raised voice, a door closing too hard, the particular silence that preceded the worst evenings: none of these were reliable cues, because sometimes they meant nothing at all, and sometimes they meant everything. What his body absorbed was not a single catastrophic event but a long education in the impossibility of safety.

He did not seek help during childhood or adolescence. He was, by most external measures, a high-functioning young man — academically driven, earnest, and eventually the youngest principal his district had appointed. But the past did not recede. Instead, it reorganised itself.

When Kofi tries to sit down and deliberately reconstruct what happened to him — to form a coherent account he could tell a therapist or write in a journal — he finds the memory strangely inaccessible, as though it belongs to someone else or exists behind frosted glass. And yet it arrives uninvited in fragments: the particular texture of a floor, a quality of light, a physical sensation in his chest that belongs to no present moment. These pieces do not assemble into a narrative. They surface and then subside, leaving him disoriented. What disturbs him most is that when these fragments do come, they carry a vividness that his ordinary memories do not — more present, more insistent, more real than his memory of last Tuesday or last year's graduation ceremony.

Old photographs are among the most reliable triggers. A colleague recently brought a childhood album to a staff appreciation event, and Kofi found himself unable to stay in the room. He said he needed to check on something in his office. In truth, the images — any images of children in domestic settings — pulled at something he could not name and did not want to approach. Waking from nightmares is its own particular difficulty; the residue of those nights clings through the morning, and on those days he arrives at school already exhausted and braced. And unpredictability — a student's sudden outburst in the hallway, a meeting that goes off-script, a plan that collapses — produces in him a vigilance that is entirely disproportionate to the situation, though he cannot always explain that to himself or others.

What frightens Kofi most, and what he returned to repeatedly in early sessions, is his anger. He has not harmed anyone. But he is certain that the capacity for something terrible lives inside him — that whatever was done to him has altered him at a fundamental level, and that the alteration is permanent. He has come to believe that he is not the person he would have been, that something was taken that cannot be restored. Alongside this sits a quieter but equally persistent conviction: that bad things will find him regardless of what he does, that his efforts to build safety — the career, the relationship, the carefully maintained composure — are ultimately insufficient. His partner has noticed his withdrawal on difficult mornings and has asked, more than once, whether something is wrong. He has not been able to answer honestly.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a moment in his own school hallway when he raised his voice at a student — not severely, not harmfully, but more than he intended — and saw the child flinch. He drove home that evening and sat in his car for a long time. He is most afraid of becoming something he recognises. He is most hoping to be told that he is not already there.
